title: cracking-rosetta algorithm entry
description: One curated algorithm in data/algorithms/. This schema documents the shape for editors and external consumers; tools/validate.pl is what actually gates a PR, because the checks that matter most (does hashcat mode 2811 exist in this hashcat? does dynamic_12 exist in this john?) are cross-references no schema can express.

id.description: Stable identifier. MUST equal the filename stem; it is what external automation keys on, so it never changes once published.

name.description: Human-readable name, as an SME would say it.

aliases.description: Other names this algorithm is known by, for search.

expression.description: hx-style expression, e.g. md5(md5($p).$s). The semantic join key: it is what lets a validator assert two tools' identifiers denote the same construction.

expression_proof.description: The tier on expression:, in the same vocabulary the per-tool blocks use, because it is the same kind of claim. An expression is a statement about what the algorithm IS, and validate.pl fails a build when two entries share one - so a key whose provenance cannot be audited is a key that will eventually have to be weakened. 'vector' means the expression string itself was compiled by john --format=dynamic='...' and recovered this entry's own plaintext from its own hash. 'upstream' means a project that verifies by recomputation stated it - john's own --list=subformats for a locally proven identifier. 'asserted' means a human said so. 'absent' means this algorithm has no expression in the dynamic language at all, which is a decision worth recording once rather than re-asking every run; pair it with denotation:.

verified.description: Same four tiers, same meanings as a per-tool block.

verified_at.description: ISO date the tier was last established. Never promote a tier without re-running the check.

verified_with.description: Version string of whatever established it, e.g. the john build.

note.description: Why, when the tier is not self-explanatory - especially for 'absent'.

denotation.description: How people refer to this algorithm when there is no machine-checkable expression: a pseudo-expression in a language richer than john's dynamic ('hmac("sha1", $plain, $salt)', 'md5(base64_encode($plain))'), or simply the label a suite or a standard uses ('PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256', '7-Zip'). It is deliberately NOT tiered, because nothing can round-trip it; instead it carries a source, so it is never an unattributed human claim. Illegal alongside expression:, which would make the entry say the same thing twice in two strengths.

text.description: The denotation itself, exactly as the source spells it.

source.description: Where the wording came from. 'sheet' is the migrated Google Sheet; a tool name means it restates that tool's own label, which is then also in tools.<tool>.

note.description: Anything a reader needs in order to trust or qualify it.

category.description: The human axis this entry sits on. primitive: one hash function over the plaintext. composite: a construction over several. iterated: another entry applied N times. encoding: another entry's digest written differently. application: a product's use of a computation another entry also names. protocol: a challenge-response or wire format. kdf: a deliberately slow derivation.

application.description: The product this row is about, when category is 'application' - Joomla, vBulletin, osCommerce. Data rather than punctuation inside name:.

application_version.description: Version constraint the product places on the row, e.g. '>=3.8.5'.

relations.description: Typed edges to other entries. Many-to-many and symmetric: every edge must be mirrored on the entry it names. This is what lets two entries share an expression honestly - the edge says they are the same computation and the distinction says why both rows exist.

kind.description: same-computation: identical bytes in, identical bytes out. encodes: same digest, different textual encoding. input-encoding: same primitive over a re-encoded plaintext. iterates: this entry is the other applied N times. truncates: this entry is the other, cut short. collides-on-subset: agrees only on a degenerate class of inputs, so a tool may crack one entry's vector without denoting it. duplicate-of: no distinction survives and one of these should go.

entry.description: The id of the other entry.

distinction.description: Why both rows exist despite the relation. 'none' is legal only with kind duplicate-of, which is how a merge is proposed in data rather than in a comment. 'naming' is the weakest distinction and says nothing about the algorithm: the tools publish several identifiers for one computation (mdxfind alone has MD4UTF16, NTLM and NTLMH for md4(utf16($p))), and each row is where a reader arrives from a different name. Use it only where a curator has looked at a proposed duplicate and decided both names should keep a row of their own; a machine proposing a merge still writes duplicate-of.

status.description: needs-review marks an entry a machine created and a human has not yet confirmed - what the upstream-drift PRs emit. merged marks a TOMBSTONE: the entry lost a merge, its content now lives on the entry merged_into names, and this file survives only so the published id keeps resolving - it is a filename stem, a URL fragment in docs/index.html and the key in dist/rosetta.csv. A tombstone asserts nothing: no tools, vectors, expression, denotation or category, and validate.pl excludes it from every coverage count.

merged_into.description: Required by status: merged and illegal without it. The id of the surviving entry this one was folded into, stated as data so a consumer can follow it without parsing the relations prose. The survivor must exist and must not itself be a tombstone - chains are rejected, so a second merge repoints the first tombstone rather than lengthening a trail.

iterations.description: mdxfind -i value. Part of the identity, not a tuning knob: MD5x02 is john's dynamic_2 and MD5x03 is dynamic_3, so the same type at a different iteration count is a different algorithm.

crack.description: Alec Muffett's Crack, historical reference only. Crack delegates to the host crypt(3) and implements nothing itself; see docs/REFERENCES.md.

vectors.description: Test vectors. A vector is what promotes a mapping to tier 'vector'. Where two tools expect different serializations of one credential, both strings live here, grouped by credential: and distinguished by which tools reads_in says actually read each. form: says which serialization each string is, and the native form is primary over any tool's rewriting of it.

source.description: Where this vector came from: hashcat, mdxfind, john, sheet, or a person.

form.description: Which serialization this string is written in. 'native' is the form the producing system itself stores or emits; a tool name is that tool's own spelling of the same credential. The native form is PRIMARY even where no cracking tool reads it - a tool that rewrites a credential to suit its parser has not changed what the credential is. Primacy is therefore derived and never asserted: within a credential: group the native vector is the primary one, and an entry may hold at most one. An entry carrying a native vector must say in notes: what that form is shaped like.

reads_in.description: Which tools were PROVEN to read this exact string, written by tools/verify-vectors.pl and never by hand. A tool is listed only when it loaded and cracked this serialization under an identifier this entry names; it is removed when every identifier of that tool ran and none did; and the vector is left alone when the tool did not run, because a tool that was not run says nothing. Where one vector reads in two tools they agree on the format; where an entry needs one vector per tool they do not, which is what makes a divergent serialization discoverable.

credential.description: Groups vectors that are ONE credential written in different tools' serializations. Two vectors sharing a credential are not independent evidence and must never be read as corroboration. An entry holding a group of more than one must say in notes: how the forms differ and that the re-encoding was proven rather than assumed.

legacy.description: Identifiers from services that no longer exist. Kept because they make old cracking write-ups readable, not because anything can be verified against them.

tier.description: vector: round-tripped locally by that tool under that exact identifier - the only tier meaning proven. upstream: asserted by a project that verifies by recomputation. asserted: a human said so. absent: the tool does not support this algorithm.
